bib.title: A Dirty Dozen: Twelve Common Metric Interpretation Pitfalls in Online Controlled Experiments

question: Which metric interpretation mistakes recur in online controlled experiments at Microsoft, and how can they be detected or avoided?
contributions: Twelve metric interpretation pitfalls, each with a real-experiment example and detection/avoidance guidance
A metric taxonomy: Data Quality, OEC, Guardrail, Local Feature/Diagnostic metrics

results.claim: Opening links in a new tab raised MSN.com homepage Page Load Time by 8.32% because 7.8% fewer (faster, cached back-button) homepage loads were in treatment: a metric sample ratio mismatch.
results.setup: MSN.com homepage experiment, new tab vs same tab on link click; p<=0.05
results.quote: The results showed 8.32% increase in Page Load Time (PLT)
results.note: Same experiment reports 7.8% fewer home page loads in treatment.

results.claim: Treatment had 7.8% fewer homepage loads than control, so the PLT metric was computed over different sets of page loads.
results.quote: with the treatment having 7.8% fewer home page loads then the control

results.claim: Moving an MSN module higher cut its per-user CTR by 40% although the experiment was good: impressions rose 200%, clicks 74%, page CTR flat, revenue up.
results.setup: MSN.com module repositioned from near bottom to higher position; users balanced
results.quote: The result showed a 40% decrease in CTR of the module

results.claim: Denominator (module impressions) rose 200% and numerator (clicks) 74% in the module-move experiment.
Underpowered page-views-per-user metric: a 0.5% increase was not significant; only a 7.8% or larger change was detectable at 80% power, CI about +-5%.
results.setup: MSN.com experiment, total page views per user
results.quote: only 7.8% or larger change could be detected with 80% power

results.claim: A Bing OEC metric with p=0.029 failed to replicate in a certification rerun with double the traffic.
results.setup: Bing.com experiment, key OEC metric of user satisfaction; rerun with double traffic showed no significant change

results.claim: A new Bing ad algorithm raised revenue 2.3% and cut ads per page 0.6% overall, but ads per page rose 0.3% on original pages and fell 2.3% on dup pages, so the goal of keeping ad load was not met.
results.setup: Bing ad auction and placement experiment, segmented original vs dup pages

results.claim: A coach-mark experiment showed +0.96% whole-page clicks and +2.07% top-sites clicks, but the effect decayed daily and vanished after the first visit (novelty effect).
results.setup: Edge new tab page, 4-week experiment, coach mark shown once to users with empty top sites
results.quote: The experiment result showed 0.96% increase in whole page clicks

results.claim: Replacing the Outlook.com button with a mail-app button gave +4.7% navigation clicks and +28% button clicks, but no retention or satisfaction change and decaying daily clicks; the experiment was shut down.
results.quote: we saw a 4.7% increase in overall navigation clicks on the page

results.claim: A Windows Store top-selling apps configuration showed an unexpected 10% increase in views caused by misconfigured pages that showed no content.
results.quote: unexpected 10% increase in the number of views of one type

limits: Examples are single experiments from Microsoft products (MSN, Bing, Skype, Xbox, Edge, Windows Store) with no aggregate prevalence data.
Authors say the twelve are by no means the complete list.
Experiment sizes, durations and user counts are mostly not given; mitigations such as Fisher's method, Bayesian monitoring and HTE tools are named without detail or evidence.
Segment example (5.8) reports significance but no effect sizes.
practices: Automatically detect sample ratio mismatch with a chi-square test on treatment/control user counts and treat SRM as invalidating the experiment (Sec 4).
Decompose a metric into numerator and denominator and sub-parts when a metric-level SRM occurs (Sec 5.1).
Always report numerator and denominator count metrics alongside any ratio metric (Sec 5.2).
Prefer average of per-user ratios over ratio of averages (Sec 5.2).
Create a Data Quality loss-rate metric for every client event, measured against a server event or via sequence numbers; prefer server-side events (Sec 5.3).
Run an a priori power analysis for OEC and guardrail metrics; aim for at least 80% power (Sec 5.4).
Do not read a non-significant underpowered metric as no change (Sec 5.4).
Rerun with larger traffic when OEC metrics have borderline p-values; emphasise strongly significant metrics (Sec 5.5).
Make ship decisions only at the pre-defined time point, or use adjusted p-values or Bayesian testing for continuous monitoring (Sec 5.6).
Auto-detect heterogeneous treatment effects across segments (Sec 5.7).
Run an SRM test on each segment group, and apply Bonferroni correction when analysing segments (Sec 5.8).
Add a Data Quality metric counting values affected by outlier handling, and ensure filtering hits all variants equally (Sec 5.9).
Segment treatment effect by day or visit to detect novelty and primacy effects (Sec 5.10).
For funnels, compare success rates at each step, both conditional and unconditional, with adequately powered step metrics (Sec 5.11).
Apply Twyman's law: investigate any unexpectedly large movement, positive or negative; use automated alerts and auto-shutdown (Sec 5.12).

terms.definition: the actual ratio of users in treatment to control differs from the expected ratio (chi-square test); most of the time implies a severe selection bias
the set of events over which a metric is computed differs between treatment and control, which usually invalidates the metric
the metrics used to judge the experiment outcome, usually leading metrics measurable in short duration and indicative of long-term value
metrics not clearly indicative of success but which must not be significantly harmed when making a ship decision
a short-term positive treatment effect that fades over time
a treatment effect that appears small at first and grows as users learn or the ML system adapts
any figure that looks interesting or different is usually wrong
conditional: proportion completing a step among users who attempted it; unconditional: over all users who started at the top of the funnel
